items.followUp: Explain the significance of crossing over during meiosis.

rubric.why: Identifies the chromatids involved in crossing over.
rubric.description: States that crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the chromatids involved and their homologous chromosomes together or by a clear equivalent description.

rubric.why: Describes the exchange that occurs and/or identifies chiasmata as its visible site.
rubric.description: Explains that chromatids exchange corresponding segments and that the points where they cross are called chiasmata.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the segment exchange and naming or correctly describing chiasmata.

modelAnswer: During prophase I of meiosis, non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange corresponding segments; this is called crossing over.
The points where the chromatids cross and remain attached are called chiasmata.

items.followUp: State two differences between photosynthesis and cellular respiration.

rubric.why: Shows that photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water to form food and oxygen.
rubric.description: States the materials used and products formed in photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly showing photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water and produces glucose and oxygen.

rubric.why: Shows the reverse material changes in respiration.
rubric.description: States that respiration uses glucose and oxygen and forms carbon dioxide and water, releasing energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing the reactants and products of respiration; energy release may also be stated.

modelAnswer: In photosynthesis, carbon dioxide and water are used to make glucose and oxygen, storing light energy in glucose.
In respiration, glucose and oxygen are broken down to form carbon dioxide and water, releasing energy; therefore, the material changes are opposite.

items.followUp: State the number of phosphate groups in ATP and ADP, and explain which stores more usable energy.

rubric.why: Identifies ATP as having three phosphate groups.
rubric.description: States that ATP contains three phosphate groups.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating the number of phosphate groups in ATP.

rubric.why: Identifies ADP as having two phosphate groups and less stored energy than ATP.
rubric.description: States that ADP has two phosphate groups and that ATP stores more usable energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the ADP phosphate-group difference and/or its lower energy store compared with ATP.

modelAnswer: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) has three phosphate groups and stores more usable energy.
ADP (adenosine diphosphate) has two phosphate groups and stores less energy than ATP.

items.followUp: Describe how the enzyme-substrate complex helps an enzyme speed up a reaction.

rubric.why: Recognizes that the substrate binds to the enzyme's active site.
rubric.description: States that the substrate binds at the enzyme's active site, forming an enzyme-substrate complex.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing substrate binding or formation of the enzyme-substrate complex.

rubric.why: Identifies the effect of enzyme action on the reaction energy barrier.
rubric.description: Explains that this interaction provides a route with lower activation energy, speeding the reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that enzymes lower the activation energy or provide an equivalent lower-energy pathway.

modelAnswer: The substrate binds to the enzyme's active site, forming an enzyme-substrate complex.
This provides a reaction pathway with lower activation energy, so the reaction proceeds faster.

items.followUp: Define nutrients and nutrition, giving one example of a nutrient.

rubric.why: Defines nutrients as substances needed by an organism.
rubric.description: Defines nutrients as substances required for energy, growth, repair or other life processes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable definition of nutrients.

rubric.why: Distinguishes nutrition as a process rather than a substance.
rubric.description: Defines nutrition as the process of obtaining and using nutrients.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining nutrition as the process of obtaining and utilizing nutrients.

modelAnswer: Nutrients are substances required by an organism for energy, growth, repair and other life processes.
Nutrition is the process by which an organism obtains and utilizes nutrients.

items.followUp: What are micronutrients? Give one example required by plants.

rubric.why: Gives the defining feature of macronutrients.
rubric.description: Defines macronutrients as nutrients required in large amounts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they are required in large amounts or quantities.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example of a plant macronutrient.
rubric.description: Gives an example such as nitrogen, phosphorus or potassium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any valid example of a macronutrient.

modelAnswer: Macronutrients are nutrients required by plants in large amounts.
Examples include nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

items.followUp: Explain how the structure of a root hair helps it absorb water from the soil.

rubric.why: Explains how root hairs increase the area available for absorption.
rubric.description: States that root hairs provide a large surface area for water absorption.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking root hairs with an increased absorptive surface area.

rubric.why: Identifies osmosis as the process by which water enters root hairs.
rubric.description: States that water moves from the soil into root hair cells by osmosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying osmosis as the method of water uptake.

modelAnswer: Root hairs greatly increase the surface area of the root in contact with the soil.
Water enters the root hair cells from the soil by osmosis.

items.followUp: Name four environmental factors that affect the rate of transpiration.

rubric.why: Assesses whether the student can name multiple factors influencing transpiration.
rubric.description: Names four relevant factors, such as light intensity, temperature, humidity, wind, water availability or leaf area.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for four valid factors; award 1 mark for two or three valid factors.

modelAnswer: Factors affecting the rate of transpiration include light intensity, temperature, humidity, wind velocity and water availability.
Leaf area also affects the rate of transpiration.
